topics.title: Intro to drama: style of a one-woman play
topics.html:
• Monodrama: one actress plays Emily for the whole play. Every other character (husband, children, mother-in-law, servants, guests) is unseen. We only hear Emily's side of every conversation
  • Direct address: Emily speaks to the audience as if we were her guests, friends or family. We are drawn in and become her listeners
  • Flashbacks and time shifts: the play moves back and forth in time instead of telling the story in order
PartTimeWhat we see
Act 1 opens1950Emily at her peak: capable manager of the house, fond mother, society hostess
Act 1 flashback1920s–1929Her childhood and early marriage: how powerless and vulnerable she once was
Act 2 openslate 1950sThen flashes back to her "glory days" of the early 1930s
Act 2 returnslate 1950sCooking babi buah keluak; Kheong tries to break away; the family crisis
Final sceneold ageIn modern Singapore her memory drifts free of time and rewrites the past as she wished it had been

Effect of the structure: like meeting a new friend, we learn Emily's story in pieces, and the most private details come last. We admire her first, then understand why she needs control, then see what it costs.

Watch out: because we only hear Emily, she is an unreliable narrator. Say "Emily claims…" or "Emily presents herself as…" when her version may not be the whole truth.

topics.title: Context: setting and atmosphere
topics.html:
• Playwright: Stella Kon, a Singaporean writer. She began the play in 1982 and it won first prize at the 1983 National Playwriting Competition
  • First staged: 1984 in Seremban, Malaysia (actress Leow Puay Tin), then at the 1985 Singapore Drama Festival with Margaret Chan as Emily
  • Inspiration: Kon's grandmother, who lived in a house called Oberon on Emerald Hill. Kon said she was the model for Emily's character, but not for the events of her life
  • Setting: Emily's big family house, Oberon, on Emerald Hill (off Orchard Road), from 1929 to Emily's old age in modern Singapore
  • Peranakan world: Straits Chinese families who mixed Chinese and Malay culture: Baba Malay language, sarong kebaya, nyonya food, large households run by a matriarch
  • It is often called Singapore's most-staged play and a landmark of Singapore theatre in English
SettingAtmosphere it creates
The grand house at Emerald Hill, full of guests, food and servantswealth, pride, busy and lively; Emily is in charge
A big extended family under one roof (in-laws, cousins, children)competitive and tense; everyone watches everyone
Emily's early married lifelonely and hostile: "So they tried to bully me but I didn't cry" (p. 11)
Hospital, empty house, old age in modern Singaporesad, quiet, lonely; the old world is fading
Using context in an answerLink it to a point, in one sentence: "In a 1930s Peranakan family, a wife's worth came from serving her husband's family, so Emily's careful pleasing of her mother-in-law is how she gains security and power."
Watch out: don't write a history paragraph. One sentence of context, tied to the question, is enough.

topics.title: Plot in order (what really happened)
topics.html:
1. Childhood: Emily's father dies. When she is about 10, her mother leaves her, complaining that she has only a "useless" daughter and no son. Emily is passed between relatives
  2. 1929, age 14: she marries her cousin Kheong, about twice her age, and moves into the wealthy Gan household at Oberon, Emerald Hill
  3. Winning the house: she pleases her mother-in-law (making tea, preparing betel leaves, massaging her at card games) and is rewarded with a diamond ring. Step by step she takes over running the household
  4. Matriarch and hostess: by the 1930s–1950s she is a famous hostess and the real power in the family. Children: Richard (eldest, her favourite), Edward, Charlie and Doris
  5. Kheong drifts away: her husband has a mistress, Diana Lee, and stays at her house. Emily still sends him food (p. 39), then exposes him (p. 40). When he is in hospital he refuses to see her (pp. 43–44)
  6. Richard: Emily plans his future for him ("I have written to a college in London for you", p. 17). In England he wants to give up his studies and work at a riding school; Emily immediately phones the riding school to stop him. Unable to live the life she has planned for him, Richard takes his own life
  7. Doris: wants to marry an American, Steve Jackson. This time Emily lets her go: she has learnt that love means letting go
  8. Old age: on Charlie's advice she sells most of the Emerald Hill land (p. 52). Nieces and nephews still visit "the old auntie" (p. 49). Alone in a changed Singapore, she remembers and rewrites her past
Watch out: the play does not show these in this order (see Form and structure). In an essay, refer to moments by what happens ("when Emily goes to London…"), not by page number.

topics.title: Peranakan culture and language in the play
topics.html:
Word or detailMeaningWhy it matters
Nyonya / BabaPeranakan woman / manEmily's identity as a proud nyonya
Baba MalayPeranakan language mixing Malay and HokkienEmily switches between English and Baba Malay: shows her world and her many roles
Sarong kebayatraditional embroidered blouse and sarongcostume that marks her status and tradition
Babi buah keluakpork cooked with black keluak nutsEmily's cooking shows skill and control; food is how she wins love and loyalty
Sireh (betel leaves)chewed by older nyonyaspreparing it for her mother-in-law shows how she pleases those with power
The house, Oberonbig family home on Emerald Hillher kingdom: the space she controls
  • Food, festivals, clothes and family rules show a traditional world that is fading by the end, as Singapore modernises and her children look to the West
Watch out: don't just list cultural details. Say what each one shows about Emily (status, control, love, change).

topics.title: Drama terms to use in answers
topics.html:

Watch out: naming a term earns nothing on its own. Always add its effect: "The direct address makes the audience feel like Emily's confidants, so we sympathise with her even when she is manipulative."

topics.title: Impressions of Emily: Act 1
topics.html:
In Act 1 we meet Emily at the height of her power, in her own home.

ImpressionEvidenceWhat it shows
Sociable, welcoming"Mr Chan, fill up your plate, Mr Chee, try a bit of sambal" (p. party scene)a warm, confident hostess who talks easily to everyone
Commanding"After all in six weeks you will have gone to England and you will lose touch with him anyway" (p. 6); then orders her servant Ah Hoon aroundshe takes charge of everyone, even her children's friendships
Responsible, organised"So I keep myself busy, running the household, looking after all the family" (p. 7); plans the new bathroomsshe takes her duties seriously and plans in detail
Proudhuge meals, fine cutlery, the family's standingshe wants to impress and keep up the family name
Resilient (in flashback)"So they tried to bully me but I didn't cry: I never cried for myself" (p. 11)she survived a hard start; we start to sympathise
How to word an impressionUse 2–3 precise adjectives, then evidence and explanation: "Emily comes across as commanding. She tells Richard that in six weeks he 'will lose touch with him anyway' (p. 6), deciding his friendships for him, which shows she expects her word to be final."
Watch out: "hardworking and responsible" with no quote was marked as vague in class. Always add a quote and say what it shows.

topics.title: Impressions of Emily: Act 2
topics.html:
In Act 2 her control is tested, and we see her change.

ImpressionEvidenceWhat it shows
Controlling, strict"Richard, you better listen to my advice." (p. 25); she immediately phones the riding school when Richard says he will give up his studiesshe puts her plans above her son's wishes
Enraged, frustrated"I've had enough of his nonsense." (p. 40)her patience with Kheong and Diana Lee breaks
Loyal, still caring"But I send him special food from day to day" (p. 39); "Kheong! Kheong! Which ward is he in?" (p. 43)she keeps her duty as a wife, even when he no longer loves her
Hurt, vulnerable"What do you mean, he doesn't want to see me…" (p. 44)the powerful matriarch is rejected; we pity her
Changed, receptive"live your own life" (p. 48), "make your own decisions" (p. 48)after Richard's death she learns to let go

The big shift: from a woman who controls everyone (Act 1) to one who is rejected, grieves, and learns to listen (Act 2).

Watch out: an answer on "impressions" should show change. Contrast Act 1 with Act 2 rather than listing traits from one act only.

topics.title: Emily and Kheong (husband)
topics.html:
Words to describe itEvidence and explanation
Beginningdistant, cordial"I expected the father to bring him to see the Headmaster" (p. 14): Kheong "couldn't be bothered" with his children, so Emily does everything alone.
"My husband didn't know" (p. 11): she hides her hard work from him and he only asks "Emily you're all right ah?" (p. 11). Polite, but not close
Endone-sided, tense, strained"he's staying with his mistress's house" (p. 39) yet "But I send him special food from day to day" (p. 39): she keeps her duty though he has left her.
"I've had enough of his nonsense." (p. 40): tension explodes and she exposes him.
"Kheong! Kheong! Which ward is he in? Is he awake now? Can I talk to him?" (p. 43) → "What do you mean, he doesn't want to see me…" (p. 44): she still cares, he refuses her. Only Emily is trying
Watch out: don't call the marriage simply "bad". Use precise words (distant, cordial, one-sided, strained) and show how it changes.

topics.title: Emily and her children
topics.html:
Words to describe itEvidence and explanation
Beginningcontrolling, suffocating, strained, one-sided"I have written to a college in London for you to study there next year" (p. 17): she decides Richard's future without asking him.
"you will do everything that I want you to do" (p. 17): the children can't disagree.
"Richard, you better listen to my advice." (p. 25): "you better" sounds threatening.
Stage direction: she laughs as Richard flatters her (p. 5): Emily believes they are close, but this is only how she sees it
Endcaring, warm, receptive, more open about feelings"I don't forbid you to get married" (p. 48), "live your own life" (p. 48), "make your own decisions" (p. 48): she lets Doris marry and live in America.
She tells a tenant she can't renew his lease (p. 49) so Doris's family will have a home in Singapore.
"I took his advice and sold the land" (p. 52): she now listens to Charlie

Why she changes: Richard's death. She doesn't want to make the same mistake of being too controlling again.

Watch out: compare Richard (held too tightly → tragedy) with Doris (let go → a warmer bond). This contrast is the heart of the motherhood theme.

topics.title: Emily and her brothers- and sisters-in-law
topics.html:
Words to describe itEvidence and explanation
Beginninghostile, competitive, tense"So they tried to bully me but I didn't cry: I never cried for myself" (p. 11): as a young bride she was picked on.
"You tell them lah, they must show respect to their brother lah…" (p. 34): as wife of the eldest son, Kheong, she uses her status to make them show respect.
"What was Freddy's position?" (p. 36): she competes with Susie over their sons' grades, pleased when Richard beats Freddy
Endcaring, loving, on good terms"Well, how's your mother?" (p. 49): she asks after the family.
"Now and again the children come to call on me, and Mabel's children and Molly's children come to visit the old auntie" (p. 49): the families hold no grudge and send their children to visit
Watch out: the in-laws show the theme of status: Emily moves from bullied newcomer to the most powerful woman in the family, then to a respected "old auntie".

topics.title: Who's who (all unseen)
topics.html:
CharacterWhoWhat they show about Emily
Kheonghusband (and cousin), eldest son of the familyher striving pushes him away; he turns to his mistress Diana Lee
Richardeldest son, her favouriteher love becomes control; his death is the play's tragedy
Dorisdaughter, studies and marries in AmericaEmily learns to let go
Charlie (and Edward)younger sonsCharlie's advice to sell the land shows Emily now listens
Mother-in-lawhead of the house when Emily arrivesEmily learns power by pleasing her, then takes her place
Emily's motherleaves Emily as a childsource of Emily's insecurity; sons valued over daughters
Susie, Mabel, Mollysisters-in-law (Freddy is Susie's son)rivalry and status in the extended family
Diana LeeKheong's mistressa threat to Emily's position as wife
Ah HoonservantEmily's authority over the household

Because one actress plays everything through Emily's voice, we only ever get Emily's version of these people.

Watch out: spell the names right: Kheong, Doris, Richard, and the playwright Stella Kon ("Kon" in essays, not "Stella").

topics.title: Motherhood
topics.html:
Kon shows that a mother's love can turn into control, and that real love means letting go.

PointEvidence
Emily was an unloved daughter: her own mother left her, calling her a useless daughter because she wasn't a sonchildhood flashback
Motherhood gives Emily purpose and power: she runs her children's lives"So I keep myself busy, running the household, looking after all the family" (p. 7)
Love becomes control: she plans Richard's future and silences him"I have written to a college in London for you" (p. 17); "you will do everything that I want you to do" (p. 17); "Richard, you better listen to my advice." (p. 25)
The cost: Richard can't live his own life, and his death is the play's tragedythe riding school; his death
A better kind of mothering: she lets Doris choose, and quietly makes sure she has a home"live your own life" (p. 48); "make your own decisions" (p. 48); the lease (p. 49)
Model topic sentence"Kon presents motherhood as a powerful but dangerous love: Emily's devotion to Richard turns into control, and only after losing him does she learn to let Doris 'live [her] own life' (p. 48)."
Watch out: don't just say Emily is a "bad mother". Show why she controls (her own childhood, her need to be needed) and how she changes.

topics.title: Role of women in society
topics.html:
Kon shows a society where a woman's worth comes from being a wife and mother, and how Emily wins power inside those limits.

PointEvidence
Girls were valued less than sonsher mother's rejection of a "useless" daughter
Women had little choice: married at 14 into her husband's family, she starts at the bottom"So they tried to bully me but I didn't cry" (p. 11)
Power came through the home: running the house and hosting"running the household, looking after all the family" (p. 7); the sambal party scene
Status came from her husband: as wife of the eldest son she demands respect"they must show respect to their brother lah" (p. 34)
Double standard: Kheong can keep a mistress; Emily must still do her duty as a wife"But I send him special food from day to day" (p. 39)
Changing times: Doris studies and marries by her own choice in America"make your own decisions" (p. 48)

Emily sums up her strategy: if a woman's only value is as a wife and mother, be "the very devil of a wife and mother" so everyone depends on you.

Watch out: Emily is both a victim of these rules and someone who uses them to control others. The best answers show both.

topics.title: Other themes (useful links)
topics.html:
ThemeWhat Kon showsLinks to
Power and controla powerless girl gains power by pleasing, then managing, everyone; control brings success but ruins relationshipsrole of women; motherhood

Loneliness and the cost of successKheong leaves, Richard dies, the house is soldmotherhood; relationships

Watch out: the EOY briefing names motherhood and role of women in society. Use these other themes to support those two, not instead of them.

topics.title: How to write the essay question
topics.html:
1. Underline the key words in the question (e.g. "how", "powerful", "to what extent")
  2. Plan for 5 minutes: 3 points, each with a moment and a quote. Order them from beginning to end of Emily's life, or weakest to strongest
  3. Introduction (2–3 lines): answer the question directly and name your 3 ideas
  4. 3 body paragraphs using PEEL: Point → Evidence (quote) → Explain (word choice + effect on the audience) → Link to the question
  5. Conclusion (2–3 lines): your overall answer, plus what Kon wants the audience to think or feel
Model paragraph: "How does Kon present Emily as a powerful woman?"

Kon shows that Emily's power comes from making others depend on her [point]. She sums up her own philosophy: a woman should be "the very devil of a wife and mother" [evidence]. The word "devil" suggests that Emily knows her methods are ruthless, yet she says it with pride, showing that power matters more to her than being liked [explain]. Since a woman in her world had value only as a wife and mother, she turns those roles into weapons [context]. This shows that Emily's power is real but built on control rather than love [link].

Watch out: marking is holistic: a clear argument that answers the question all the way through beats a long list of points. "To what extent" means give both sides, then a clear judgement.

topics.title: Passage-based question: what makes it dramatic?
topics.html:
The passage-based question has 2 parts on a printed extract. One part is often about style: how Kon makes the passage dramatic (tense, gripping, moving for an audience).

Dramatic deviceLook forEffect on the audience
Conflict and tensionEmily against someone (Kheong, Richard, in-laws)we wait to see who wins
Sudden shifts in tone or moodcharming → angry, proud → hurtsurprise; shows her true feelings
Exclamations, rapid questions, repetition"Kheong! Kheong! Which ward is he in?" (p. 43)panic and urgency
Ellipsis, pauses"he doesn't want to see me…" (p. 44)shock; she can't finish the thought
Stage directionsshe laughs as Richard flatters her (p. 5)shows what words hide
Unseen characters, direct addressEmily answering people we can't hearwe fill the gaps and feel part of the scene
Dramatic ironywe see what Emily doesn'tpity, unease
  1. Place the extract in one sentence: when it happens and what came just before
  2. Read twice; underline 4–5 dramatic moments
  3. Answer each part in PEEL paragraphs, taking quotes from the passage, in order
  4. Label your answers (i) and (ii), or marks are deducted
Model pointKon makes the hospital scene dramatic through Emily's frantic questions, "Kheong! Kheong! Which ward is he in? Is he awake now?" (p. 43). The repeated name and rush of questions show her panic, so the audience feels the tension. This makes the next line, "he doesn't want to see me…" (p. 44), more shocking: the ellipsis shows she is too hurt to finish.
Watch out: "dramatic" doesn't mean "exciting events". Explain how Kon's choices create tension or emotion for an audience watching the play.

topics.title: Practice questions on Emily
topics.html:
One question for each topic in the EOY briefing. Try each first, then tap it to see a model plan.

25mWhat are your impressions of Emily in Act 1 and Act 2? (Essay)

Plan:

  1. Act 1: commanding and organised: "So I keep myself busy, running the household" (p. 7); orders Ah Hoon; decides Richard's friendships (p. 6)
  2. Act 2: controlling and strict as a mother: "Richard, you better listen to my advice." (p. 25); phones the riding school
  3. Act 2: hurt, then changed: "What do you mean, he doesn’t want to see me…" (p. 44); "make your own decisions" (p. 48)

Conclusion: Emily moves from a woman who controls everyone to one who learns, through loss, to let go.

Marking tip: show change across the two acts, and support each impression with a quote and explanation.

25mHow does Kon present the theme of motherhood? (Essay)

1. Emily's own mother rejected her as a useless daughter: a lack of love shapes her.
2. Controlling love: the London college (p. 17), "you will do everything that I want you to do" (p. 17), the riding school; the cost is Richard's death.
3. Letting go: Doris may "live your own life" (p. 48); Emily even arranges a home for her (p. 49).

Message: real motherly love means letting children choose.

Marking tip: compare Richard and Doris to show Kon's message, not just Emily's actions.

25mHow does Kon present the role of women in society? (Essay)

1. Limited choices: married young; bullied by in-laws (p. 11); sons valued above daughters.
2. Power through the home: running the household (p. 7), hosting, status as the eldest son's wife (p. 34).
3. Double standards and change: Kheong's mistress versus Emily's duty (p. 39); Doris's free choices in America (p. 48).

Judgement: Emily is both limited by her society and skilled at using its rules.

Marking tip: a clear line of argument through the essay matters more than the number of points (holistic marking).

25mExplore the relationship between Emily and Kheong. (Essay)

Beginning: distant but cordial: he "couldn't be bothered" with the children (p. 14); "My husband didn't know" (p. 11).
End: one-sided and strained: she sends him food though he lives with his mistress (p. 39); "I've had enough of his nonsense" (p. 40); he refuses to see her in hospital (p. 44).

Marking tip: use precise adjectives and track how the relationship changes.

10mPassage-based (sample): How does Kon make this passage dramatic? (e.g. the hospital scene, pp. 43–44)

1. Repetition and exclamations: "Kheong! Kheong!" shows panic.
2. Rapid questions: "Which ward is he in? Is he awake now? Can I talk to him?" builds urgency.
3. Sudden turn: "What do you mean, he doesn't want to see me…": the ellipsis and the shock of rejection create pity.

Marking tip: name the device, quote the passage, then explain the effect on the audience; label each part (i) or (ii).

Watch out: these are plans. In the exam, turn each point into a full PEEL paragraph.

topics.title: The 4-Quadrant Routine (use for any poem)
topics.html:
Your teachers' routine for making meaning of an unseen poem. Work round the four questions.

QuadrantMain questionSub-questions to ask
1. See
details, patterns		What do you SEE?What is happening? What is striking? What patterns (e.g. repetition) do you notice? What can you infer from the title? First impressions?
2. Mean
significance, connections		What does this MEAN / SHOW?What does the writer mean by…? Why is … significant? How does it make you think or feel? How are details, images and parts of the poem connected?
3. Writer's craft
techniques, effects		HOW does the writer do this?What literary techniques are used? What are their effects on you and the poem? How do they build the overall meaning?
4. Big idea
overall meaning, themes		What is the BIG IDEA?What is the poem about? What is the writer saying about human nature, society or the world? What do you think of it? How do your own experiences help you understand it?

See → Mean → How (craft) → Big idea

Watch out: don't stop at Quadrant 1 (describing). The marks are in Quadrants 2–4: meaning, effects and the big idea.

topics.title: Poetry techniques and their effects
topics.html:
TechniqueWhat it isEffect words to use
Imagerywords that create a picture or sensevivid, helps the reader see / hear / feel
Similecomparison with "like" or "as"emphasises a quality, makes it easy to picture
Metaphorsays one thing is anotherstronger than a simile, gives new meaning
Personificationhuman qualities given to a thingmakes it seem alive, powerful or threatening
Alliterationsame first sound repeateddraws attention; hard sounds (k, c, t) feel harsh, soft sounds (s, m) feel gentle
Onomatopoeiaa word that sounds like its meaningbrings the scene alive through sound
Repetitionword or line repeatedemphasis, insistence, strong emotion
Rhyme and rhythmsound pattern and beatregular = calm, controlled; broken = tension
Enjambmentsentence runs over the line breakspeed, flow, or an idea that can't be held back
Caesurapause in the middle of a line (punctuation)slows us down, stresses a word, hesitation
Contrasttwo opposite ideas placed togetherhighlights a difference or a change
Symbolobject standing for an ideaadds deeper meaning (e.g. a bird for hope or freedom)
Watch out: "the poet uses alliteration" scores nothing on its own. Say which words, and what the sound or picture makes the reader feel.

topics.title: Words for tone and mood
topics.html:
FeelingTone words
Happyjoyful, celebratory, light-hearted, hopeful, admiring
Sadmelancholic, mournful, regretful, nostalgic, lonely
Angrybitter, resentful, indignant, frustrated
Calmpeaceful, gentle, reflective, thoughtful
Fearfulanxious, tense, uneasy, threatening, ominous
Strongconfident, defiant, determined, proud
Mockingsarcastic, ironic, humorous
  • Tone = the speaker's attitude. Mood = the atmosphere the reader feels
  • Describe a shift: "The tone changes from hopeful to regretful in stanza 3, when…"
Watch out: avoid vague words like "sad" or "happy" alone. Pick a precise word and back it up with a quote.

topics.title: Structure and form
topics.html:
• Stanzas: how many, and does each one move the poem on (a new idea, time or feeling)?
  • Line length: short lines are quick or abrupt; long lines are slow or flowing
  • Punctuation: dashes, question marks and exclamations show hesitation, doubt or emotion
  • Opening and ending: compare them. What has changed? Is the ending a surprise, a lesson or a question?
  • Free verse (no regular rhyme or rhythm) can feel natural and like speech; a regular pattern can feel controlled or song-like
Example sentence"The poem ends with a short, separate line, which makes the final image stand out and leaves the reader thinking about the speaker's loss."
Watch out: only write about structure if you can say its effect. Counting stanzas is not analysis.

topics.title: Writing your poetry answer
topics.html:
Section B is a 2-part question, like WA3, marked holistically with the Lower Secondary Unseen Poetry band descriptors. Answer both parts and label them (i) and (ii).

Question typeHow to answer
"What do you learn about…?"one point per mark, each with a short quote
"What is the effect of…?" / "Explain the image…"name the technique, quote it, explain what it suggests and how it makes the reader feel
"How does the poet present…?" (longer)3 PEEL paragraphs moving through the poem in order, including the tone shift and the ending
PEEL paragraph frameThe poet presents [idea] as [adjective] [point]. This is seen in "[short quote]" [evidence]. The word "[one word]" suggests… which makes the reader feel… [explain]. This shows that… [link to question].
Watch out: write in the present tense and about "the poet" or "the speaker", not "I think the poem is nice".

topics.title: The Eagle (Tennyson)
topics.html:
He clasps the crag with crooked hands; Close to the sun in lonely lands, Ring'd with the azure world, he stands. The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls; He watches from his mountain walls, And like a thunderbolt he falls."The Eagle", Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1851)

Try each question first, then tap it to see the model answer.

4mWhat impressions of the eagle does the poet create in the first stanza?

The eagle seems powerful and old: "clasps" with "crooked hands" suggests a strong grip, like an old man's. It seems isolated and noble: "lonely lands" and "Close to the sun" show it lives high above everything, almost like a king.

Marking tip: two impressions, each supported with a quote and explained.

6mHow does the poet use sound and imagery to make the eagle seem powerful?

The hard "c" alliteration in "clasps the crag with crooked hands" sounds harsh and gripping, matching the eagle's strength. Personification gives it "hands", making it seem almost human and in control. From its height, "The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls": the sea, normally mighty, seems small and weak, which shows how far above the world the eagle is. The simile "like a thunderbolt he falls" ends the poem with sudden, violent speed, showing its deadly power.

Marking tip: name each technique, quote it, then explain the effect. Three developed points beat six named techniques.

4mComment on the structure of the poem.

Two stanzas of three lines, each with one rhyme sound (hands / lands / stands; crawls / walls / falls). The first stanza is still: the eagle "stands". The second ends in sudden movement: he "falls". This contrast between stillness and the final dive makes the ending dramatic.

Marking tip: link the structure to meaning: still → sudden action.

Watch out: "azure" means sky-blue. If you meet a word you don't know, work it out from context instead of skipping the line.

topics.title: “Hope” is the thing with feathers (Dickinson)
topics.html:
"Hope" is the thing with feathers - That perches in the soul - And sings the tune without the words - And never stops - at all - And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard - And sore must be the storm - That could abash the little Bird That kept so many warm - I've heard it in the chillest land - And on the strangest Sea - Yet - never - in Extremity, It asked a crumb - of me."Hope is the thing with feathers", Emily Dickinson (published 1891)
4mWhat is hope compared to, and why is this effective?

Hope is an extended metaphor for a small bird that "perches in the soul". A bird is small and light but keeps singing, which suggests hope is gentle yet always present inside us. It "sings the tune without the words": hope is a feeling we can't always explain.

Marking tip: identify the metaphor, then explain at least two ways the bird is like hope.

6mHow does the poet show that hope is strong even in hard times?

"sweetest - in the Gale": hope sounds best during a storm, so it is strongest when life is hardest. "sore must be the storm / That could abash the little Bird" means only a terrible storm could silence it, stressing its toughness. It "kept so many warm", showing it comforts many people. Finally, it "never" asked "a crumb": hope gives everything and asks for nothing. The dashes slow the reader down and stress key words like "never".

Marking tip: move through the poem in order and include the ending; comment on the dashes for a structure point.

3mDescribe the tone of the poem.

The tone is hopeful and admiring. The speaker praises hope gently, and in the last stanza becomes personal and grateful ("I've heard it").

Marking tip: a precise tone word, a quote, and a mention of the shift to the personal "I".

Watch out: stay with the metaphor. Every detail (feathers, singing, storm, crumb) is about hope, not a real bird.

topics.title: Who Has Seen the Wind? (Rossetti)
topics.html:
Who has seen the wind? Neither I nor you: But when the leaves hang trembling, The wind is passing through. Who has seen the wind? Neither you nor I: But when the trees bow down their heads, The wind is passing by."Who Has Seen the Wind?", Christina Rossetti (1872)
4mWhat is the effect of the repeated question?

Repeating "Who has seen the wind?" at the start of each stanza makes the poem sound like a riddle or a song. The answer, "Neither I nor you", reminds us that the wind is invisible, so it makes the reader think about things we can't see but know are real.

Marking tip: explain both the sound effect (song or riddle) and the idea it raises.

6mHow does the poet show the wind's presence even though it cannot be seen?

The poet shows the wind through its effects. Personification: "the leaves hang trembling" suggests the leaves are nervous or afraid, so the wind seems mysterious and powerful. "the trees bow down their heads" shows the trees bowing as if to a king, showing the wind's power and importance. The word "But" in both stanzas turns from what we can't see to what we can. The poem may suggest that unseen things such as love or faith can be known by their effects.

Marking tip: two developed points on personification, plus one on the wider meaning, scores well.

Watch out: a "deeper meaning" must come from the poem. Use "may suggest" and link it to words in the text.
